name: Glycogen storage disease type XI (Fanconi-Bickel syndrome)

clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic SLC2A2 mutations affecting GLUT2, the facilitative glucose and galactose transporter of hepatocytes, pancreatic beta cells, enterocytes and the renal proximal tubule.
Combines a hepatic glycogenosis with a generalised proximal (Fanconi-type) tubulopathy, hence the label hepatorenal glycogenosis.
Shows a characteristic paradoxical glucose pattern: fasting hypoglycaemia together with postprandial hyperglycaemia and hypergalactosaemia.
Proximal tubular dysfunction produces glucosuria, generalised aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, bicarbonate wasting (proximal renal tubular acidosis) and hypophosphataemic rickets.
Hepatomegaly and nephromegaly reflect glycogen accumulation, with a doll-like facies, protuberant abdomen and marked short stature.
Galactose intolerance can mimic classic galactosaemia and may be flagged on newborn screening.
Management is supportive: frequent feeds and uncooked cornstarch for hypoglycaemia, plus replacement of water, electrolytes, bicarbonate, phosphate and vitamin D for the rickets.
The prominent renal Fanconi syndrome and the glucose/galactose transport defect distinguish it from other glycogen storage disorders.
reference.pathophysiology: GLUT2 is a low-affinity, high-capacity facilitative transporter that mediates bidirectional movement of glucose and galactose across the membranes of hepatocytes, pancreatic islet beta cells, intestinal epithelium and renal proximal tubular cells. Loss of function traps monosaccharides within hepatocytes and tubular cells, where excess glucose is diverted into glycogen synthesis, producing glycogen-laden hepatomegaly and nephromegaly. Defective proximal tubular monosaccharide handling, together with secondary intracellular metabolic changes, drives a generalised proximal tubular dysfunction manifesting as the Fanconi syndrome. Impaired hepatic glucose release and blunted islet glucose sensing generate fasting hypoglycaemia yet postprandial hyperglycaemia and hypergalactosaemia, while impaired intestinal monosaccharide absorption contributes to gastrointestinal symptoms and poor growth.
additionalDifferentials: Nephropathic cystinosis and other causes of the renal Fanconi syndrome
Glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke), with hepatomegaly and hypoglycaemia but no Fanconi tubulopathy
Dent disease and hereditary fructose intolerance
additionalInvestigations: SLC2A2 molecular genetic testing as the confirmatory test
Urinalysis for glucosuria, generalised aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and bicarbonate loss
Serum electrolytes, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and venous blood gas or bicarbonate
Fasting and postprandial glucose and galactose profiles
Skeletal radiographs and bone densitometry to characterise rickets
Abdominal ultrasound to demonstrate hepatomegaly and nephromegaly
redFlags: Hypophosphataemic rickets with progressive skeletal deformity
Severe failure to thrive with marked growth failure
Metabolic acidosis and electrolyte disturbance from proximal tubular losses
Hypergalactosaemia flagged on newborn screening requiring urgent evaluation
reference.prognosis: With careful metabolic and renal supportive care, life expectancy is usually reasonable, although short stature and rickets are common and no curative therapy exists. Lifelong monitoring of growth, bone health and proximal tubular function is required.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as classic galactosaemia because of the hypergalactosaemia
Attributing the rickets to nutritional vitamin D deficiency alone and missing the underlying tubulopathy
Expecting the fasting-hypoglycaemia with postprandial-hyperglycaemia pattern to fit a single conventional glucose disorder
Confusing the historical use of the term GSD XI for lactate dehydrogenase deficiency with Fanconi-Bickel syndrome
references: Saudubray — Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
Scriver — The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Prevent fasting hypoglycaemia with frequent feeds and uncooked cornstarch to provide slow-release glucose
Restrict dietary galactose to limit postprandial hypergalactosaemia while ensuring adequate overall nutrition through a metabolic dietitian
Replace ongoing proximal tubular losses with oral bicarbonate or citrate, phosphate and potassium supplementation and water as needed
Treat hypophosphataemic rickets with phosphate together with active vitamin D such as alfacalcidol or calcitriol
Monitor growth, bone health, electrolytes, acid-base status and proximal tubular function over the long term
Coordinate multidisciplinary care between metabolic medicine and nephrology
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive SLC2A2 inheritance with family testing
